lesson.title: Lists Inside Lists: Understanding Nested Lists
lesson.summary: Because a list can hold any type of value, one of its elements can itself be a list, which is what programmers mean by a nested list.
lesson.body:
A list in Python does not care what type of data it holds, and it does not require every element to be the same type either. You have already stored numbers and strings in a list. Nothing stops you from storing a list as one of the elements of another list. When that happens, you have a nested list: a list where at least one element is itself a list.

This matters because it lets a single variable represent data that has structure, not just a flat row of values. A student's record might need a name, a list of grades, and a birth year all together. Nesting is how you keep that grouped without inventing extra variables for every piece.

```python
club = ["Chess Club", ["Monday", "Wednesday"], 2024]
print(club[1])
print(club[1][0])
```

This prints:

```
['Monday', 'Wednesday']
Monday
```

club[1] reaches into the outer list and pulls out element at index 1, which happens to be the inner list ['Monday', 'Wednesday']. Adding a second set of brackets, club[1][0], reaches one level deeper: it takes that inner list and grabs its element at index 0. Reading nested indexing from left to right, one bracket pair at a time, is the easiest way to keep track of which list you are currently indexing into.

One detail worth being precise about: len(club) is still 3, not 4. Python never automatically flattens a nested list, so the inner list ['Monday', 'Wednesday'] counts as exactly one element of club, regardless of how many items it holds internally. Nesting can go deeper than two levels too, a list inside a list inside a list, though in practice most nested structures you will meet in this course stop at two levels, which is exactly the case explored next as a list of lists.
